title: Baseball Analytics Engine
text:
This started as a database design exercise and turned into something I actually care about. The goal was to take raw baseball data — players, teams, games, per-game stats, and ballparks — and turn it into a normalized relational schema that could actually support real analysis instead of one giant flat spreadsheet.
Stack: MySQL, MySQL Workbench

title: Baseball Analytics Engine
text:
The Schema
Everything is connected through foreign keys instead of repeated, denormalized columns: player, team, game, playerStats, and ballpark tables each hold one kind of fact, and joins reconstruct the full picture on demand. That structure is what makes the analytical queries in the Data Exploration section possible — cleaning and modeling the data correctly up front means the downstream queries stay simple.
-- Example: a normalized fact table instead of a flat file
CREATE TABLE playerStats (
    statID INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
    playerID INT NOT NULL,
    gameID INT NOT NULL,
    atBats INT,
    hits INT,
    rbi INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (playerID) REFERENCES player(playerID),
    FOREIGN KEY (gameID) REFERENCES game(gameID)
);

title: Baseball Analytics Engine
text:
Why It Matters
Bad or unstructured data breaks everything downstream of it. Designing the schema first — deciding what belongs in its own table, what’s a foreign key vs. a duplicated string, and where the data can go inconsistent — is the unglamorous work that makes every later query trustworthy.

title: Canvas-Risk
text:
Canvas-Risk is a terminal dashboard that connects to the Canvas LMS API and flags students who are at risk of falling behind — missing work, slipping grades, and inactivity — before it’s too late in the semester to fix. It touches every layer of the stack: an external API client, a persistent database, an analytics engine on top, and an interactive UI.
Stack: Python, SQLAlchemy, SQLite, Textual, Typer

Layer

title: Canvas-Risk
text:
The Risk Engine
Each student’s failure probability is a weighted blend of signals pulled straight from the synced Canvas data — current grade, missing assignments, grade trend over time, inactivity, and how they compare to their peers:
WEIGHTS = {
    'grade': 0.40,
    'missing': 0.30,
    'trend': 0.10,
    'inactivity': 0.10,
    'peer_comparison': 0.10
}
On top of the raw score, students get tagged into a profile — High Achiever, The Ghost (inactive with missing work), Slipping, Chronic Latecomer, and so on — so a TA scanning the dashboard gets an instant read instead of just a number.

title: Canvas-Risk
text:
Why It Matters
This is the project that best represents “full stack” for me: real external data in, a proper local data model, analysis logic that turns raw numbers into a decision-ready signal, and a UI that makes it usable without touching a database client. Every layer had to work for the last one to mean anything.

title: Baseball Analytics Engine — Query Layer
text:
This is the exploration side of the Baseball Analytics Engine — once the schema was normalized, I wrote queries to pull real insight out of it: rolling performance windows, efficiency ratios, and league-wide rankings. It’s the kind of analysis you’d actually see behind a sports platform, not a one-off report.
Stack: MySQL

title: Baseball Analytics Engine — Query Layer
text:
Rolling 5-Game Batting Average
A window function partitioned per player and ordered by game date, so each row shows a trailing performance trend instead of a single-game snapshot.
SELECT
    p.firstName, p.lastName, g.gameDate, ps.hits, ps.atBats,
    ROUND(
        SUM(ps.hits) OVER (
            PARTITION BY p.playerID ORDER BY g.gameDate
            ROWS BETWEEN 4 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
        ) /
        NULLIF(SUM(ps.atBats) OVER (
            PARTITION BY p.playerID ORDER BY g.gameDate
            ROWS BETWEEN 4 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
        ), 0), 3
    ) AS rolling_5game_avg
FROM player p
JOIN playerStats ps ON p.playerID = ps.playerID
JOIN game g ON ps.gameID = g.gameID
ORDER BY p.lastName, g.gameDate DESC;

title: Baseball Analytics Engine — Query Layer
text:
League Rankings with CTEs
A CTE aggregates wins across home and away games, then RANK() orders the whole league by performance.
WITH TeamWins AS (
    SELECT teamID, COUNT(*) AS wins
    FROM (
        SELECT homeTeamID AS teamID FROM game WHERE homeTeamScore > awayTeamScore
        UNION ALL
        SELECT awayTeamID AS teamID FROM game WHERE awayTeamScore > homeTeamScore
    ) all_wins
    GROUP BY teamID
)
SELECT
    t.teamName, t.city,
    COALESCE(tw.wins, 0) AS total_wins,
    RANK() OVER (ORDER BY COALESCE(tw.wins, 0) DESC) AS league_rank
FROM team t
LEFT JOIN TeamWins tw ON t.teamID = tw.teamID
ORDER BY league_rank ASC;

title: Baseball Analytics Engine — Query Layer
text:
Other Angles Explored

RBI efficiency per hit — SUM(rbi) / SUM(hits) per player, filtered to players with a meaningful sample size
Ballpark run averages — average combined runs per game, grouped by venue

title: SwingOS
text:
SwingOS is a real-time computer vision tool that watches a baseball swing through a webcam and gives instant feedback on head movement — one of the most common mechanical breakdowns in hitting. I built it to see if I could train my body to feel correct mechanics without needing a coach standing there watching every rep.
Stack: Python, OpenCV, MediaPipe

title: SwingOS
SwingOS
text:
Why It Matters
This is applied ML in the sense that matters to me most: taking a general-purpose pretrained model (pose estimation) and wiring it into a tight feedback loop that solves a specific, real problem. The interesting part isn’t training a model — it’s turning model output into a signal a person can actually act on in the half-second it takes to swing a bat.
